facts.value: £738.6m of loans — PWLB £534.1m, LOBOs £36.2m, Salix £6.9m, WYCA £0.4m and £161.0m of short-term borrowing from other local authorities — plus £155.5m of PFI and finance leases

source.title: Annual Treasury Management Report 2025-26 — Governance and Audit Committee, 18 June 2026

facts.note: Table 5, which foots in every row and column. Total borrowing £894.1m, down £8.3m. The local authority borrowing rose £12m; 7.2 gives the reason plainly: 'due to current high PWLB interest rates the Council completed more short term borrowing with other Local Authorities'.

facts.value: £1,163.2m, up from £1,078.5m and £104.2m above the original budget of £1,059.0m

source.title: Annual Treasury Management Report 2025-26 — Governance and Audit Committee, 18 June 2026

facts.note: Table 2, which foots in both actual columns. £155.5m of it is PFI and finance leases. Driven by £93.0m of capitalised revenue costs and £28.6m of unfinanced capital expenditure, less £25.7m of MRP and £12.2m of PFI and lease repayments.

source.title: Annual Treasury Management Report 2025-26 — Governance and Audit Committee, 18 June 2026

facts.note: Table 3. The identity closes exactly: CFR £1,163.2m less total borrowing £894.1m less other liabilities £3.2m = £265.9m, the printed figure. The prior year closes too.

facts.value: 28% of borrowing matures within twelve months against a 30% upper limit — two percentage points of headroom

source.title: Annual Treasury Management Report 2025-26 — Governance and Audit Committee, 18 June 2026

facts.note: Table 8 and Appendix 1. The maturity structure sums to 100% and every other bucket is far inside its limit (12%, 12%, 11%, 7%, 13%, 6%, 11% against limits of 20%, 50%, 50%, 90%, 90%, 90%, 90%). 9.2: 'Debts under 12 months have remained high reflecting that the Council has used short temp borrowing to mitigate against fixing into higher rate longer term loans.' 7.4 already flags the cost: 'Increased short term borrowing in 2025-26 will mean higher interest costs which has been included in the 2026-27 budget.'

facts.value: £56.4m of PWLB matured at an average 6.1% and £50m was drawn at an average 4.45% — about 165 basis points, or £0.83m a year on the £50m

source.title: Annual Treasury Management Report 2025-26 — Governance and Audit Committee, 18 June 2026

facts.note: Section 7.3 and Table 6, which prints all four loans: £10m at 4.51% for 2 years, £10m at 4.52% for 3.5 years, £20m at 4.47% for 1.5 years and £10m at 4.31% for 1 year. They sum to £50.0m and reblend to 4.456% against the stated 4.45%.

facts.value: a Capitalisation Direction of £113.0m ran through 2025-26 capital expenditure, reduced from an original £127.0m (2024-25: £120.0m)

source.title: Annual Treasury Management Report 2025-26 — Governance and Audit Committee, 18 June 2026

facts.note: Sections 2.5 and 2.8, and Table 1. Total capital expenditure was £219.8m against an original £279.7m. §2.8: the Direction is funded 'either from capital receipts or by setting aside minimum revenue provision (MRP) over 20 years as specified in MHCLG's Statutory MRP Guidance (2024 edition).' Capital financing costs are 15.3% of net revenue stream (Table 4), expected to settle around 14% in the medium term.

source.title: Annual Treasury Management Report 2025-26 — Governance and Audit Committee, 18 June 2026

Separately, £31.7m of investment property across about 240 properties returning 3.1% against a 5.00% benchmark — 14.6 says 'certain investment property is included in the asset disposal programme' — and £0.7m of loans to third parties earning £22k.

summary.text:
Bradford publishes a treasury contact with an address, so it is email-ready. Our PWLB file holds 68 loans at £534,113,717 against their Table 5 PWLB row of £534.1m — to the pound — and all 68 are maturity profile, which is what their own 6.2 says the strategy is. Tables 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 8 and 12 all foot, and the balance sheet identity closes exactly in both years: CFR £1,163.2m less £894.1m of borrowing less £3.2m of other liabilities is the £265.9m of under-borrowing they print.

The lead is £161.0m of short-term borrowing from other local authorities, up £12m, with 7.2 giving the reason without hedging — PWLB rates are high, so they went to the inter-authority market. That is one of the largest local authority borrowings in our file, and it is why the under-twelve-month bucket sits at 28% against a 30% upper limit: two percentage points of headroom on a £738.6m book. Paragraph 7.4 already flags the cost into the 2026-27 budget.

The good news in the same story is the refinancing. £56.4m of PWLB matured at an average 6.1% and £50m was drawn at an average 4.45% across four loans of one to three and a half years — 165 basis points, about £0.83m a year, and Table 6 prints every loan so the average checks (4.456%).

At the other end of the book sit three PWLB loans of £6,483,704 each at 9.13%, running to January 2027, 2028 and 2029 — the highest cluster of legacy coupons in the library, and part of why 32 of the 68 loans still price above par. The other 35 carry £64.8m of discount, for about £59.2m net today. Also of record: a Capitalisation Direction of £113.0m, reduced from £127.0m, with MRP over 20 years under the 2024 Guidance.

officer.meeting: Governance and Audit Committee — mid-year treasury update due winter 2026

market.basis: MATURITY profile, CERTAINTY rates (published standard less 0.20)

courses_named: PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator
officer.body:
Hi Lynsey,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the annual report that went to Governance and Audit on 18 June. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first. We hold 68 PWLB loans for Bradford totalling £534,113,717, against the £534.1m in your Table 5 — to the pound. All 68 are maturity profile, which is exactly what your 6.2 describes. Table 5 foots in every row and column including the movement column, Table 2 foots in both actual columns, and the balance sheet closes precisely in both years: CFR £1,163.2m less £894.1m of borrowing less £3.2m of other liabilities is the £265.9m of under-borrowing in Table 3.

We wrote because of two numbers that sit next to each other.

The first is £161.0m of short-term borrowing from other local authorities, up £12m, and your 7.2 says why without hedging it: PWLB rates are high, so you went to the inter-authority market instead. That is one of the largest local authority borrowings in everything we have read this year.

The second is the 28% in your maturity table, against a 30% upper limit. Two percentage points of headroom on a £738.6m loan book — about £15m — while every other bucket sits far inside its limit: 12% against 20, 12% against 50, 11% against 50, and single figures against 90. It is not a breach and your 9.2 explains the logic plainly. It is simply the tightest single indicator in the report, and it is tight because of the first number rather than anything else.

What makes that worth a line is where the inter-authority market has been. Across everything we have read, pricing over this year end ran from about 4.15% to 8.50%: Gloucestershire borrowed £55m at 4.15% to 4.70%, while Cornwall paid 8.50% for four days, Harlow 7.75% for a month, and Bexley paid Herefordshire 7.00% for 32 days. That is a four hundred basis point range in one market in one winter, and it widens exactly when PWLB months are thin — July was thin, £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%. No council can see that distribution from its own trades, which is why we publish it, at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity. Your 7.4 has already put the higher cost into the 2026-27 budget, so the question is the shape of the market you roll into rather than whether the cost is recognised.

The good news is in the same section and deserves saying. £56.4m of PWLB matured at an average 6.1% and £50m was drawn at an average 4.45% — 165 basis points, roughly £0.83m a year. And Table 6 prints all four loans, so the average can actually be checked rather than taken on trust; we rebuilt it and it comes to 4.456%. Most reports state the average and leave it there.

One more thing, at the other end of the book. You still hold three PWLB loans of £6,483,704 each at 9.13%, running to January 2027, 2028 and 2029. Those are the highest coupons we have found in any council's file, and they are part of why 32 of your 68 loans still price above par even on today's curve. The other 35 carry about £64.8m of discount, so the book nets to roughly £59.2m of discount. Your 11.1 says the roughly 1% differential between new borrowing and premature repayment rates made rescheduling unviable in the year, which was the right read at the time. We're not suggesting anything follows now: we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote. The point is only that the differential moves, and yours is priced daily at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

On training, four fit Bradford. Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets and LA Credit Analysis go to the £161m. Liquidity & cashflow forecasting goes to the 28% bucket. PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator covers 11.1 and the 9.13% loans. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
